## Understanding the ggplot:

The ggplot system is base don the idea that :\
A plot is built by a combination of independent components (like a sentence in a language):\
Every plot is made of :

- Data

- Aesthetics(aes)

- Geometry (geom\_\*)

- Statistical transformation(stat)

- Scales

- Themes

  Think of ggplot as layers of transparent sheets.

```{r}
# Let's load the required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggsignif)
library(scales)
```

### Let's load the insurance data set

```{r}
df <- read_csv("insurance.csv",
               show_col_types = FALSE)
cat("Data Loaded Successfully")
```

```{r}
utils::head(df,3)
```

**Note** :\
ggplot automatically groups data when a categorical variable is mapped to an aesthetic like color, shape, or linetype.

```{r fig.dpi=300, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
ggplot(
  data = df,
  mapping = aes(x = bmi, y = charges)
)+
  geom_point(mapping = aes(color = smoker))+
  labs(
    x = "bmi(kg/m^2)",
    y = "Charges($)",
    title = "Relationship between bmi and insurance charges",
    color = "Smoker Status"
  )+
  theme_bw()
```

### **Global Mapping Vs Local mapping :**

variables can be mapped to aesthetics locally or globally: When you map a variable to an aesthetic in the ggplot() function, that applies globally. it means any other layer added assumes those set featutures or mapping in ggplot.\
For instance, we could map cyl(cylinders) to color in mtcars globally in ggplot aes() or locally in aes() in geom_point:

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width= 10, fig.height = 5}
# local mapping of color and global mapping of x and y axis
ggplot(mtcars,
       aes(x = wt, y = mpg)
       )+
  geom_point(aes(color = cyl))+ # this applies only to geom_point
  theme_bw()
```

### Settings and Mapping:

There is a difference between settings and Mapping:Mapping connects variables in the data set to visual aesthetics,whiles settings assigns visual properties independent of the data.\
.Mapping are usually declared in aesthetics but settings are not.\
**NB: ggplot function itself doesn't accept color settings: You can only use aesthetics for mapping to variables: If you want one unique color be set, use it in any of geom\_\* function**

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width= 10, fig.height = 5}
# setting color : You see how every point is blue
ggplot(mtcars,
       aes(x = wt, y = mpg)
       )+
  geom_point(color = "blue") # color is set to one color: blue

```

### Let's add another layer:

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width= 10, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(
  mtcars, aes(wt,mpg)
)+
  geom_point(
    aes( color = factor(cyl))
    )+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              formula = y ~ x, 
              se = FALSE)
```

**Local vs Global Aesthetic Definitions:\
Local definition**

colors are only available for geom_point(). Any added layer will not have these colors and x, y mappings\
declared on in geom_point()

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width= 10, fig.height = 5}
# let's define the data globally in ggplot and aesthetics locally in geom_point()
ggplot(mtcars)+
  geom_point(aes(wt,mpg,color = cyl))
```

**Global definition of aesthetics and data:**

You by now see that the two plots are the same. This sis because aesthetics can be defined both globally or locally. You see that geom_point() inherits the coloring of point based on cyl from ggplot() aesthetics

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width= 10, fig.height = 5}
# let's define the data and aesthetics all in ggplot
ggplot(mtcars,
       aes(wt,mpg, color = cyl))+
  geom_point()

```

#### **Aesthetic inheritance and overriding:**

Aesthetics declared globally can be overridden with settings: Here we globally map our x and y variables in ggplot(). And then geom_point() inherits the coloring and x, y mapping. So points get colored by cyl as mapped in ggplot().\
Also we add a first geom_smooth which equally inherits the x,y aesthetics but with color, settings it override the globally mapped color = cyl.\
We add yet another geom_smooth() layer and that one is allowed to inherit all global mappings.

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.height = 5, fig.width =10}
# Let's demonstrate something more complex
ggplot(
  mtcars,
  aes(hp,mpg,color = factor(cyl))
  )+
geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(
    color = "black",
    method = "lm",
    formula = y~x,
    se = FALSE
  )+
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y~x,
    se = FALSE
  )+
  labs(
    title = "inheriting and overidding global mapping"
  )
 
```

### Facet Wrapping:

Facet wrapping helps in splitting figures based on categories: Let's do a scatter plot of hp over mpg and then facet wrap by cyl: Color becomes redundant when faceting by the same variable, because each panel already represents a single category. Removing color from geom_point() won't make any difference

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.height= 5, fig.width = 10}
ggplot(
  mtcars,
  aes(hp,mpg)
)+
  geom_point(
    aes(color = factor(cyl))
  )+
  facet_wrap(~cyl)
```

**Let's take another example:**

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.height= 5, fig.width = 10}
ggplot(
  mtcars,
  aes(wt,mpg)
)+
  geom_point(
    aes(color = factor(cyl))
  )+
  geom_smooth(
    color = "lightblue",
    method = "lm",
    formula = y~x,
    se = FALSE
  )+
  facet_wrap(~gear, nrow =1) # you can use nrow to specify number of rows you want
```

### Facet Grid:

Facet grid is used to split the figure into multiple small figures based on two variables. Unlike facet wrap which takes only one variable, facet grid works on two variables:

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.height = 5,fig.width = 10}
ggplot(
  df,
  aes(x= bmi, y = charges)
)+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(
    color = "lightpink",
    method = "lm",
    formula = y~x,
    se = FALSE
  )+
  facet_grid(sex~smoker) # this forms a grid with sex as rows and smoker as column
  
```

### More Customization:

### Labels and Themes:

labs() : This controls what text appears on the graph: axis titles, shapes, color and size titles, graph title, subtitle, caption and many more properties.

theme() : This is for styling, it controls where these labels should be positioned, orientation,coloring, font size, font style and so on.\
Let's work on some examples: We are going a little deeper this time

```{r fig.dpi=300, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
ggplot(
  df,
  aes(bmi,charges,color = smoker)
)+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y~x,
    se = FALSE
  )+
  labs(
     x = "bmi(kg/m^2)",
     y = "Charges($)",
     color = "Smoker",
     title = "Relationship between bmi and insurance charge",
     subtitle = "Relationship stratified by smoker status",
     caption = "Source : SambugAnalytics"
  )+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = 'serif', size =13),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "grey40"),
    axis.title = element_text(size =12, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = 'right',
    legend.title = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 12)
  )

```

### More customization of plots : Bar and Pie Charts

#### Basic bar chart:

Let's take a look at the distribution of regions in the insurance data set: Let's start with a basic bar chart and then we progress:

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width =10, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(
  df, aes(x = region)
)+
  geom_bar(
    fill = "lightblue", # color to fill bars
    width = 0.5,        # width of bar
    )+
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of region",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Count",
    subtitle = "Distribution of region by gender",
    caption = "SambugAnalytics(World bank Data)"
  )+
  theme_bw()
  
```

#### Grouped_bar chart : Let's see the distribution of sex across the regions:

Here two most important things matter.\
1. Fill : Determines how the bars are filled , you can map the bars to a fill in aesthetics\
2.Position : Determines how the bars are presented, either stacked, grouped or overlap\
3. coord_flip() : This is added like a layer to create a horizontal bar chart\
There different positions : **dodge, stack, fill, identify**

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width = 10, fig.height =5}
# Here is a well customized grouped bar
ggplot(
  df, aes(x = region, fill = sex)
)+
  geom_bar(
    width = 0.5,
    position = "dodge" # position each sex bar side by side(group)
    )+
  # adding bar labels
  geom_text(
    stat = "count", # specify the statistics used in geom_bar: that is count
    aes(label = after_stat(count)), #set's the internal count variable as bar label
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), # position must match geom_bar position
    vjust = -0.4 # vertical adjustment
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of region",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Count",
    subtitle = "Distribution of region by gender",
    caption = "SambugAnalytics(World bank Data)"
  )+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif",size =13),# global text style
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold",hjust = 0), 
    axis.title.x = element_text(size =11, face = "bold"),# styles only x axis title
    axis.title.y = element_text(face = "bold",size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

**Geom_col() :**

You can equally use this for bar chart but used only when you have summarized the data already.\
In that case you already have your computed count, y already. geom_bar is not needed to do the computation. it is just like setting stat to identity in geom_bar.

```{r}
# Grouping data for plotting
grouped <- df |> 
  count(region,sex)
grouped
```

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width = 10, fig.height =5}
# using geom_col
ggplot(
  grouped, aes(x = region,y =n, fill = sex)
)+
  geom_col(
    width = 0.5,
    position = "dodge" # position each sex bar side by side(group)
    )+
  # adding bar labels
  geom_text(
    aes(label = n), # sets the count as bar label
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), # position must match geom_bar position
    vjust = -0.4 # vertical adjustment
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of region",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Count",
    subtitle = "Distribution of region by gender",
    caption = "SambugAnalytics(World bank Data)"
  )+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif",size =13),# global text style
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold",hjust = 0), 
    axis.title.x = element_text(size =11, face = "bold"),# styles only x axis title
    axis.title.y = element_text(face = "bold",size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

**Stacked Bar:**

The only thing we are going to change is the position: we are going to set it to 'stack'

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width = 10, fig.height =5}
# Here is a well customized grouped bar
ggplot(
  df, aes(x = region)
)+
  geom_bar(
    aes(fill = sex), # fills each main bar by the variable sex
    width = 0.5,
    position = "stack" # position each sex bar side by side(group)
    )+
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of region",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Count",
    subtitle = "Distribution of region by gender",
    caption = "SambugAnalytics(World bank Data)"
  )+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif",size =13),# global text style
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold",hjust = 0),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size =11, face = "bold"),# styles only x axis title
    axis.title.y = element_text(face = "bold",size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

```

\*\*Say we wanted percentages as our labels in the grouped bar (geom_col or geom_bar)\*\* I am going to use the grouped data:

```{r}
grouped_per <- grouped |> 
  mutate(
    percent = round((n/sum(n))*100,1)
  )
grouped_per
```

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width =10, fig.height = 5}
# let' do the plotting now 
ggplot(
  grouped_per,
  aes(x = region, y = percent, fill = sex)
)+
  geom_col(
    position = "dodge",
    width = 0.5
  )+
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percent,"%")),# paste0()combines strings without a space btn
    position = position_dodge(width =0.5),
    vjust = -0.4
  )+ 
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of region",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Percent",
    subtitle = "Distribution of region by gender",
    caption = "SambugAnalytics(World bank Data)"
    )+
  theme_bw()+
   theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif",size =13),# global text style
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold",hjust = 0), 
    axis.title.x = element_text(size =11, face = "bold"),# styles only x axis title
    axis.title.y = element_text(face = "bold",size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
  
```

### **Box Plot:**

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(x = region, y = charges)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    aes( fill = smoker),
    position = position_dodge(width=0.3), # controls sapce between subplots
    width = 0.3, # controls size of boxplot
    staplewidth = 0.4, # controls cap of whiskers
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 0.5,
    coef = 1.5,
    median.linewidth = 1, # controls thickness of median line
    outlier.color = "red",
    outlier.size = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Insurance Charges by Smoking Status",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Charges",
    caption = "Source: SambugAnalytics"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    text = element_text(family= "serif",size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(face = 'bold')
  )
```

### **Adding Significance Levels to Box plots**

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width = 10, fig.height =5}
ggplot(
  df,
  aes(x=region, y = charges)
)+
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "white",
    width = 0.2,
    median.linewidth = 1,
    staplewidth = 0.5,
    alpha =1,
    color = 'black',
    linewidth= 1,
    coef = 1.5,
    outlier.color = 'black',
    outlier.size = 1.5
  )+
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,80000))+ # setting  y limit
  geom_signif(
    comparisons = list(c("northeast","northwest"),c('southeast','southwest')),
    annotations = c("NS","NS"),
    y_position = 70000
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of insurance charges by region",
    caption = "Source:SambugAnalytics",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Insurance charges( $ )"
  )+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif",size =13),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
  
```

**Three ways to control axis limits:**

1.  using xlim() and ylim()
2.  using coord_cartesian(xlim = c(x1,x2), ylim= c(y1,y2)
3.  scale_x_continous(limit = c(x1,x2, breaks = seq(2,20,2) and scale_y_contionous(limit =c(y1,y2), breaks = seq(2,18,2))

### [**Distribution plots: Histogram and Density Plots**]{.underline}

#### Histogram:

```{r fig.dpi= 300, fig.height= 7, fig.width= 14}
# let's look at the distribution of bmi in our study participants 
bw <- (max(df$charges) - min(df$charges)) / 30
ggplot(
  df,
  aes(x = charges)
)+
  geom_histogram(
    aes(fill = smoker),# showing distribution by smoker status
    bins = 30,
    color = "white",
    binwidth = bw # you can use bins or binwidth but not both
      )+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,200))+ # controls y limit
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(min(df$charges),
                 max(df$charges), by = bw), # controls xlimit plus break
    labels = scales::comma
    )+
  labs(
    x = "Charges ranges",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Distribution of charges across participants"
  )+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

**A quick note, you can pass on specific data manipulated to the geom aesthetics and it will override the data called in ggplot().**

Let's look at an example with the mpg data: say we want to highlight 2seaters data points in a scatter plot of displ against hwy

```{r}
utils::head(mpg)
```

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.height= 7, fig.width= 14}
# Now the graph
ggplot(
  mpg, aes(x=displ, y = hwy)
)+
  geom_point()+
  geom_point(
    data = mpg |> filter(class=="2seater"),
    color = 'red', # colors the edges of the points 
    size = 3,
    shape = 21,
    fill = "red"
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Highlighting 2seater points",
    caption = "Souce : Sambuganalytics"
  )+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = 'serif',size = 13),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

### **Density Plot:**

Density plots are used together with histograms for distribution analysis:

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width=14, fig.height= 7}
ggplot(
  df,
  aes(bmi)
)+
  geom_density(
    color = 'black',
    fill = "green", # fills in the area under the distribution 
    alpha = 0.05  # controls color intensity of this geom elements
  )+
  labs(
    title = 'Distribution of bmi',
    caption = "Source: Sambuganalytics"
  )+
  theme_bw()
```

**We could show distribution by a category :**

Say i want to show distribution of bmi across smoker status:

```{r fig.dpi = 300, fig.width=14, fig.height= 7}
ggplot(
  df,
  aes(bmi)
)+
  geom_density(
    aes(color = smoker, fill = smoker),
    alpha = 0.05  # controls color intensity of this geom elements
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of bmi across smoker status",
    caption = "Source : Sambuganalytics"
  )+
  theme_bw()
```

### **Let's use geom_density_ridge()**

Note that unlike geom_density, geom_denstiy_ridge() requires x and y argument. x is the continous variable whose distribution is of interest and y is the category on which the distribution is split.

```{r fig.dpi=300, fig.height= 5, fig.width = 10}
# loading ggridges library
library(ggridges)

# Now our plot 
ggplot(
  df,
  aes(x = bmi, y = smoker)
)+
  geom_density_ridges(
    aes(fill = smoker),
    alpha = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  )+
  labs(
    
  )
  theme_bw()
```
